lessons.body:
Performance Budgets and Measurement

A performance budget turns “fast enough” into a falsifiable statement. TaskFlow separates browser
experience, API latency, database behavior, and capacity. The exact numbers below are starting
engineering targets for this course, not universal guarantees.

Boundary                                                        TaskFlow starting budget

Core Web Vitals                                                 p75 LCP <= 2.5 s, INP <= 200 ms, CLS <= 0.1

GET /tasks                                                      p95 API <= 300 ms under normal target load

PATCH /tasks/:id                                                p95 API <= 400 ms under normal target load

Error rate                                                      < 1% unexpected 5xx during benchmark

DB query hot path                                               Investigate repeated queries above ~100 ms and any
obvious N+1 pattern

Bundle                                                          No unexplained large client-bundle regression after
dependency changes

Core Web Vitals measure user-visible browser experience and are evaluated at the 75th percentile. They
do not replace backend metrics. A fast API can still produce poor LCP because the browser downloaded
too much JavaScript, and a tiny JavaScript bundle cannot compensate for a two-second database query.

Field browser           route/renderi                             repository/Pri                             infrastructure
API latency                                 PostgreSQL
metrics                 ng                                        sma                                        saturation
→                   →                    →                      →                   →

Figure 2. Separate performance layers

Production caution: Never benchmark development mode. Use production builds, representative data,
warm-up, fixed scenarios, and the same environment before comparing two changes.

lessons.body:
Next.js Rendering, Bundles, and Core Web
Vitals

Next.js already gives TaskFlow useful performance defaults: Server Components do not add client
JavaScript, routes are code-split, and static assets can be cached. Performance work therefore starts by
preserving those defaults rather than immediately adding client-side state or heavy libraries.

Client JavaScript checklist
• Keep "use client" boundaries as low as practical. A client boundary pulls its imported component
subtree into the client bundle.

• Lazy-load interaction-heavy Client Components or third-party libraries that are not needed for initial
render.

• Use next/font to self-host/optimize fonts and next/image where image optimization is relevant.

• Measure bundles after dependency changes rather than assuming tree shaking solved everything.

• Avoid calling a Next.js Route Handler from a Server Component when the Server Component can call
the backend/data source directly; that adds another server hop.
// next.config.performance.ts
import bundleAnalyzer from "@next/bundle-analyzer";

const withBundleAnalyzer = bundleAnalyzer({
enabled: process.env.ANALYZE === "true",
});

export default withBundleAnalyzer({});

// PowerShell
$env:ANALYZE="true"
pnpm --filter web build

The first optimization question is not “what can I memoize?” It is usually “why is this code in the client
bundle at all?”
Key idea: LCP, INP, and CLS are field-facing outcomes. Bundle size, hydration cost, and render waterfalls
are causes you investigate, not goals in isolation.

lessons.body:
TanStack Query Network and Render
Efficiency

TanStack Query already provides structural sharing and tracked-property render optimizations. TaskFlow
should tune freshness and invalidation based on how quickly each resource actually becomes stale
rather than globally increasing staleTime to hide network activity.

Problem                                            Better response

Every mount refetches immediately                  Choose a justified staleTime for that resource

Polling duplicates Realtime                        Use one freshness mechanism intentionally

Huge query payload                                 Reduce API projection / pagination size

Component rerenders on unused query state          Avoid object-rest destructuring that defeats tracked-property
optimization

Mutation invalidates everything                    Invalidate the smallest correct query family

const taskListOptions = (query: TaskListQuery) =>
queryOptions({
queryKey: taskKeys.list(query),
queryFn: () => fetchTasks(query),
staleTime: 30_000,
placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
});

A cache is not free memory. Large result sets cost JSON transfer, parsing, reconciliation, and browser
memory even if they avoid another request. Pagination and narrow API response shapes are still primary
performance tools.
Production caution: Do not increase staleTime simply to make a network panel look quiet. That trades
freshness for fewer requests and must match the product requirement.

lessons.body:
NestJS + Fastify API Hot Path

NestJS with Fastify is already a strong baseline. Most TaskFlow API latency will usually come from
database/network work, serialization volume, or repeated application operations rather than the
controller decorator itself. Measure before rewriting architecture.

HTTP                                     controller/ser
validation                             repository/DB        serialization       response
parse/auth                               vice
→                  →                    →                    →                   →

Figure 3. API latency decomposition

High-value checks
• Measure p50/p95/p99 per normalized route.

• Avoid synchronous CPU-heavy work on request paths; move report/PDF/import processing to workers
when it becomes long-running.

• Return only fields the client needs. Large JSON responses cost DB I/O, serialization, bandwidth, parsing,
and memory.

• Prefer native Fastify integrations on hot paths rather than generic middleware when performance
matters.

• If you adopt Fastify response JSON schemas later, benchmark them in the real NestJS integration rather
than assuming the theoretical gain applies unchanged.

Fastify documents that response schemas can substantially improve JSON serialization throughput.
TaskFlow does not replace the Zod/Nest response architecture merely for microbenchmarks; it first
profiles whether response serialization is actually a meaningful share of latency.
Key idea: The optimization order should usually be: remove unnecessary work, reduce round
trips/payload, improve database plan, fix saturation, then consider lower-level framework tuning.

Prisma Query Shape, N+1, and
Overfetching

Prisma performance depends more on query shape than on whether code lives in a repository.
Repository Pattern improves organization, but it does not automatically produce efficient SQL.

N assignee/project       many database round
1 Task list query                    loop over N Tasks
queries                  trips
→                                  →                         →

Figure 4. N+1 smell

// Prefer one intentional query shape when the UI needs related data.
const tasks = await prisma.task.findMany({
where,
select: {
id: true,
title: true,
status: true,
priority: true,
assignee: {
select: { id: true, displayName: true },
},
},
take: query.pageSize,
});

Repository review questions
• Does a list endpoint execute one bounded query shape or one query per row?

• Are we selecting large unused columns/relations?

• Are count and data queries both required for this screen?

• Does authorization scoping force expensive relation traversal that deserves an index?

• Is the same lookup repeated inside one request and safe to reuse?

Prisma currently recommends one reusable PrismaClient per process because multiple clients create
multiple pools. It also explicitly calls out N+1 as a common query-performance problem.
Production caution: Do not hide N+1 behind Promise.all. Concurrent N+1 is still N+1 and may put even
more pressure on the connection pool.

lessons.body:
PostgreSQL EXPLAIN, Indexes, and
Pagination

Indexes are workload-specific. PostgreSQL can only choose well when statistics describe the data and the
index matches real predicates/order patterns. Phase 31 teaches evidence-first index design: observe a
slow query, capture its plan, change one thing, and compare.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, title, status, priority, "createdAt"
FROM "Task"
WHERE "projectId" = $1
AND status = $2
ORDER BY "createdAt" DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0;

Plan signal                                           Question

Seq Scan                                              Is table small, predicate unselective, or useful index missing?

Index Scan / Bitmap                                   Does chosen index align with actual filter/order?

Rows estimate vs actual                               Are planner statistics inaccurate?

Buffers                                               Is query reading far more pages than expected?

Sort                                                  Could ordering be supported by a useful index, or is sort
cheap enough already?

PostgreSQL 18 documents that multicolumn B-tree indexes are most effective when constraints apply to
leading columns and recommends using multicolumn indexes sparingly. For the TaskFlow query above,
an index such as (projectId, status, createdAt DESC, id) is a candidate to measure, not a rule to apply
blindly.

Deep pagination
Offset pagination is excellent for page-number navigation, but very deep OFFSET values require
PostgreSQL to walk past earlier rows. If TaskFlow evolves into an infinite activity feed, cursor/keyset
pagination becomes a better candidate.
Production caution: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. Be careful with UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT
in production; use transactions/rollback or safe replicas where appropriate.

lessons.body:
Connection Pooling and Supabase
Topology

Database connections are finite resources. TaskFlow already runs a persistent NestJS API, so the right
pool strategy differs from short-lived serverless functions. Pooling must be sized to deployment topology,
replica count, database limits, and workload rather than copied from a blog post.

Supavisor/PgBouncer       PostgreSQL max
NestJS replica(s)                    application-side pool
when needed               connections
→                                 →                          →

Figure 5. Connection layers

• Reuse one PrismaClient / adapter per application process.

• A long-running API may use a direct/session-style connection plus its application-side pool when
network/topology supports it.

• Horizontally scaled/serverless workloads often need a server-side pooler to avoid connection storms.

• Supabase transaction pooling uses port 6543 and has session-state/prepared-statement limitations;
Prisma requires the pooler-compatible configuration documented for that mode.

• Budget connections across all API replicas plus Auth, Storage/Realtime infrastructure, migrations,
admin tools, and operational headroom.

Supabase currently distinguishes application-side pools from server-side poolers such as Supavisor. It
specifically recommends server-side transaction pooling for workloads that create many short-lived
connections.
Key idea: Increasing connection count can make a database slower if it simply allows more concurrent
work than CPU/I/O can sustain. Measure queueing and saturation, not just connection errors.

Caching, Compression, Data Locality, and
Background Work

Caching is useful when it removes repeated expensive work and the invalidation model is understood. It
is dangerous when it hides unclear ownership or serves stale private data across users/tenants.

Layer                                                 Good candidates

Browser / Next.js                                     immutable assets, route output where semantics permit,
optimized images/fonts

TanStack Query                                        authenticated server state with intentional staleTime

API/application                                       expensive repeatable public/reference reads only after
measurement

Database                                              buffer cache is automatic; optimize query/index before
inventing app cache

CDN/Storage                                           public/static content; private files require correct
signed-access semantics

Compression and payload size
Compression helps large textual payloads, but reducing payload size at the source is better: paginate,
project only required fields, avoid repeated metadata, and do not return large nested graphs the UI
never renders.

Data locality
Network latency is physics. Deploy the API near PostgreSQL when possible; keep
storage/database/service regions intentional. A beautifully optimized query still feels slow if every
request crosses continents unnecessarily.

Move slow work off the request path
PDF generation, large imports, exports, email batches, payroll/report generation, and image processing
should eventually become background jobs when their duration or retry needs exceed an interactive
request budget. The API should enqueue, return status, and let workers perform the expensive job.

Load Testing with Autocannon

Load testing answers a different question from unit/integration testing: how does the assembled system
behave when many requests overlap? Phase 31 uses autocannon because it is simple, scriptable,
Node-friendly, and sufficient for learning repeatable HTTP load experiments.
# PowerShell - run against a production-like local/staging build
pnpm dlx autocannon@8.0.0 `
-c 20 `
-d 30 `
-m GET `
-H "Authorization=Bearer $env:TASKFLOW_TOKEN" `
"http://localhost:3001/tasks?page=1&pageSize=20"

Record more than requests/second
Measure                                                  Why

p50 / p95 / p99 latency                                  Tail behavior matters to users

throughput                                               How much useful work completes

non-2xx / errors                                         Fast failures are not success

CPU / memory / event loop                                Find application saturation

DB connections / query latency                           Find persistence saturation

payload bytes                                            Understand bandwidth/serialization cost

Use a warm-up run, fixed dataset, fixed concurrency/duration, production build, and consistent
environment. Change one variable at a time. Keep benchmark results with commit/release information
so comparisons are reproducible.

authorization, define limits, and prefer isolated staging/performance environments.

lessons.body:
Performance Regression Testing and CI
Budgets

Performance tests become useful when they can detect meaningful regressions without creating flaky
gates. TaskFlow separates deterministic budgets from noisy environment-dependent benchmarks.

• Bundle-size reports can be compared in CI because build artifacts are relatively deterministic.

• Query-count assertions can catch accidental N+1 regressions in integration tests.

• EXPLAIN plan snapshots can be reviewed, but avoid brittle exact-cost assertions across
environments/data changes.

• Microbenchmarks should run on controlled hardware and are poor generic cloud-CI gates.

• End-to-end latency load tests belong in a stable benchmark environment; compare distributions, not
one request.
// Example budget metadata - illustrative
{
"route": "GET /tasks",
"scenario": "20 concurrent users / 30s",
"p95MsTarget": 300,
"unexpected5xxPercentMax": 1
}

Phase 30 observability remains the production regression detector. Synthetic benchmark results explain
capacity in a scenario; field telemetry tells you what real users are experiencing.
Key idea: A performance gate should fail on a material regression you understand, not on random cloud
noise. Otherwise teams learn to ignore or disable it.

Performance Debugging Case Studies

Case 1 - GET /tasks p95 jumps from 220 ms to 950 ms
Trace shows 780 ms in PostgreSQL. Query logs reveal a new assignee lookup per Task row. Fix the N+1
query shape, rerun integration tests, EXPLAIN the new SQL, then repeat the same load scenario. Do not
start by memoizing React components.

Case 2 - API is 90 ms but page LCP is 4.1 s
Bundle analysis reveals a large chart/editor library imported through a high-level client shell even though
the Tasks screen does not use it initially. Move the client boundary lower and lazy-load the feature.
Confirm with production build and field/lab browser measurements.

Case 3 - latency rises only at concurrency 100
Single-request traces look healthy. Under load, DB connection wait time rises and API p99 explodes.
Review replica count, application pool size, Supabase pooler mode, Postgres max connections, query
duration, and CPU/I/O saturation. More connections are not automatically the fix.

Case 4 - pagination gets slower on
OFFSET work grows with depth. Keep offset pagination for ordinary admin tables, but use cursor/keyset
pagination for deep sequential feeds where jumping to arbitrary page numbers is not required.
Key idea: Performance debugging is hypothesis-driven: locate the boundary first, then optimize that
boundary. The stack is too large for random tuning to be reliable.

Question                                                  Exit requirement

Do we know our budgets?                                   Yes - documented per layer

Can we reproduce benchmarks?                              Yes - scenario, dataset, build, concurrency, duration

lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 31: Performance

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
measure baseline -> locate bottleneck -> form hypothesis -> change one thing -> remeasure -> add regression guard

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Optimizing from intuition only

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Performance

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 31 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Measure TaskFlow and improve bottlenecks systematically across browser, API, database, cache, and network without sacrificing correctness.

Required artifact
Before/after performance report with measured bottleneck, change, and regression guard.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can produce a baseline.
• Can identify bottleneck layer.
• Can read basic query-plan evidence.
• Can justify performance tradeoffs with measurements.

Independent build sequence
1. Choose a user-visible flow and collect a baseline instead of optimizing globally.
2. Inspect network waterfalls/payloads and frontend rendering for avoidable work.
3. Measure API endpoint latency with enough context to separate application and database time.
4. Inspect PostgreSQL EXPLAIN/ANALYZE for a representative slow query and validate index/query changes.
5. Reduce N+1 or redundant requests before adding caches.
6. Record the before/after result and add a budget/test where a regression would matter.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 31: Performance. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

# Benchmark runbook
1. Build/run production mode; never compare next dev.
2. Reset/seed representative data.
3. Confirm test environment, commit, versions, region, and DB topology.
4. Warm up.
5. Run the exact same scenario (route, token role, concurrency, duration, dataset).
6. Record p50/p95/p99, throughput, non-2xx, CPU/memory, DB latency/connections.
7. Change one variable.
8. Repeat.
9. Keep change only if improvement is meaningful and correctness/security tests pass.

# TaskFlow performance budget (starting targets)

These are course targets, not universal SLAs. Revisit after production field data exists.

- Core Web Vitals at p75: LCP <= 2.5 s, INP <= 200 ms, CLS <= 0.1.
- GET /tasks p95 API latency <= 300 ms under the recorded normal-load scenario.
- PATCH /tasks/:id p95 <= 400 ms under the recorded normal-load scenario.
- Unexpected 5xx under benchmark <= 1%.
- Query review required for repeated hot-path queries around/above 100 ms or any N+1 pattern.
- No unexplained client bundle regression after dependency changes.

# TaskFlow Phase 31 performance snapshot
Study snapshot only. Performance changes must be measured before/after in the same scenario. Keep correctness, authorization, data isolation, and security tests green.

# Phase 31 version lock
- Prisma remains course-locked at 7.9.1.
- PostgreSQL 18 documentation is used for planner/index guidance.
- @next/bundle-analyzer 16.3.5 (optional development tool; keep aligned with your Next.js release line).
- autocannon 8.0.0 (benchmark tool).

# API hot-path notes
1. Remove unnecessary I/O before micro-optimizing framework code.
2. Keep payloads bounded and projections intentional.
3. Move long-running reports/imports/exports to background workers when the request budget is exceeded.
4. Do not solve DB saturation by blindly increasing connection counts.

-- Run ANALYZE first when appropriate so planner statistics are current.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, title, status, priority, "createdAt"
FROM "Task"
WHERE "projectId" = '00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001'::uuid
  AND status = 'IN_PROGRESS'
ORDER BY "createdAt" DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0;

-- Candidate only. Measure before/after; do not blindly add indexes.
-- CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ... ON "Task" ("projectId", status, "createdAt" DESC, id);

# Requires a valid bearer token in TASKFLOW_TOKEN.
# Run against a disposable/staging environment you are authorized to load test.
pnpm dlx autocannon@8.0.0 `
  -c 20 `
  -d 30 `
  -m GET `
  -H "Authorization=Bearer $env:TASKFLOW_TOKEN" `
  "http://localhost:3001/tasks?page=1&pageSize=20"

# Performance verification matrix
- Compare production builds, never development mode.
- Record commit, dataset, environment, concurrency, duration, and auth role.
- GET /tasks benchmark captures p50/p95/p99, throughput, errors.
- PATCH /tasks/:id benchmark uses a safe repeatable fixture/workflow.
- Query count check catches accidental N+1 behavior.
- EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) recorded for hot Task list query.
- Index change measured before/after and validated with correctness tests.
- DB connection usage observed during load.
- Bundle analyzer run after dependency/client-boundary changes.
- Core Web Vitals lab measurement paired with field telemetry when available.
- Security/authorization tests remain green after optimization.
